OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-i-k-2-lo.statement: Identify human senses and sensory organs.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-i-k-2-eu.statement: People experience the world through sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-i-3-5-eu.statement: Some animals experience the world differently than people do.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-i-6-8-lo.statement: Give examples of how humans combine information from multiple modalities.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-i-6-8-eu.statement: People can exploit correlations between senses, such as sight and sound, to make sense of ambiguous signals.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-i-9-12-lo.statement: N/A for AI purposes at this band.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-i-9-12-eu.statement: This topic has already been adequately addressed in the lower grade bands.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-ii-k-2-lo.statement: Locate and identify sensors (camera, microphone) on computers, phones, robots, and other devices.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-ii-k-2-eu.statement: Computers "see" through video cameras and "hear" through microphones.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-ii-3-5-lo.statement: Illustrate how computer sensing differs from human sensing.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-ii-3-5-eu.statement: Most computers have no sense of taste, smell, or touch, but they can sense some things that humans can't, such as infrared emissions, extremely low or high frequency sounds, or magnetism.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-ii-6-8-lo.statement: Give examples of how intelligent agents combine information from multiple sensors.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-ii-6-8-eu.statement: Self driving cars combine computer vision with radar or lidar imaging, GPS measurement, and accelerometer data to form a detailed representation of the environment and their motion through it.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-ii-9-12-lo.statement: Describe the limitations and advantages of various types of computer sensors.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-ii-9-12-eu.statement: Sensors are devices that measure physical phenomena such as light, sound, temperature, or pressure.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-iii-3-5-lo.statement: Explain how images are represented digitally in a computer.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-iii-3-5-eu.statement: Images are encoded as 2D arrays of pixels, where each pixel is a number indicating the brightness of that piece of the image, or an RGB value indicating the brightness of the red, green, and blue components of that piece.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-iii-6-8-lo.statement: Explain how sounds are represented digitally in a computer.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-iii-6-8-eu.statement: Sounds are digitally encoded by sampling the waveform at discrete points (typically several thousand samples per second), yielding a series of numbers.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-iii-9-12-lo.statement: Explain how radar, lidar, GPS, and accelerometer data are represented.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-a-iii-9-12-eu.statement: Radar and lidar do depth imaging: each pixel is a depth value. GPS triangulates position using satellite signals and gives a location as longitude and latitude. Accelerometers measure acceleration in 3 orthogonal dimensions.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-i-k-2-lo.statement: Give examples of intelligent vs. nonintelligent machines and discuss what makes a machine intelligent.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-i-k-2-eu.statement: Many machines use sensors, but not all use them intelligently. Non-intelligent machines are limited to simple sensing. Intelligent machines demonstrate perception.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-i-3-5-lo.statement: Use a software tool such as a speech transcription or visual object recognition demo to demonstrate machine perception, and explain why this is perception rather than mere sensing.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-i-3-5-eu.statement: Perception is the extraction of meaning from sensory signals.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-i-6-8-lo.statement: Give examples of different types of computer perception that can extract meaning from sensory signals.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-i-6-8-eu.statement: There are many specialized algorithms for perceptual tasks, such as face detection, facial expression recognition, object recognition, obstacle detection, speech recognition, vocal stress measurement, music recognition, etc.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-i-9-12-lo.statement: Explain perception algorithms and how they are used in real-world applications.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-i-9-12-eu.statement: Many devices and services rely on specialized perception algorithms, e.g., license plate readers, zip code readers, face-based phone unlocking, tagging people in Facebook posts, object identification (e.g., Google Lens), or voice-based customer service.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-ii-k-2-lo.statement: Give examples of features one would look for if one wanted to recognize a certain class of objects (e.g., cats) in an image.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-ii-k-2-eu.statement: The visual features of an object include its subparts, textures, and colors.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-ii-3-5-lo.statement: Illustrate how face detection works by extracting facial features.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-ii-3-5-eu.statement: Face detectors use special algorithms to look for eyes, noses, mouths, and jaw lines.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-ii-6-8-lo.statement: Illustrate the concept of feature extraction from images by simulating an edge detector.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-ii-6-8-eu.statement: Locations and orientations of edges in an image are features that can be detected by looking for specific arrangements of light and dark pixels in a small (local) area.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-ii-9-12-lo.statement: Explain how features are extracted from waveforms and images.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-ii-9-12-eu.statement: A speech spectrogram shows the energy present in a waveform in various frequency bands. Formants are auditory features defined as regions of concentrated energy in the spectrogram. Feature extraction from images begins with detecting edges in the image, or intensity gradients at multiple scales.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-iii-k-2-lo.statement: Describe the different sounds that make up one's spoken language, and for every vowel sound, give a word containing that sound.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-iii-k-2-eu.statement: In order for a computer to understand speech, it has to be able to recognize the sounds from which words are constructed.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-iii-3-5-lo.statement: Illustrate how sequences of sounds can be recognized as candidate words, even if some sounds are unclear.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-iii-3-5-eu.statement: Going from sounds to words is one step in the abstraction pipeline for speech understanding.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-iii-6-8-lo.statement: Illustrate how sequences of words can be recognized as phrases, even if some of the words are unclear, by looking at how the words fit together.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-iii-6-8-eu.statement: Information at higher levels of representation can be used to resolve ambiguities in lower levels of the language abstraction pipeline.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-iii-9-12-lo.statement: Illustrate the abstraction hierarchy for speech understanding, from waveforms to sentences, showing how knowledge at each level is used to resolve ambiguities in the levels below.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-iii-9-12-eu.statement: The spoken language hierarchy is: waveforms -> articulatory gestures -> sounds -> morphemes -> words -> phrases -> sentences.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-iv-k-2-lo.statement: Demonstrate figure/ground segmentation by identifying the foreground figures and the background in an image.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-iv-k-2-eu.statement: Visual scenes have a structure that includes a background and a foreground, with foreground objects partially occluding (blocking) the background.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-iv-3-5-lo.statement: Illustrate how the outlines of partially occluded (blocked) objects in an image differ from the real shapes of the objects.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-iv-3-5-eu.statement: Understanding complex scenes requires taking into account the effects of occlusion when attempting to recognize objects.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-iv-6-8-lo.statement: Describe how edge detectors can be composed to form more complex feature detectors, e.g., for letters or shapes.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-iv-6-8-eu.statement: The progression from signal to meaning takes place in stages, with increasingly complex features extracted at each stage.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-iv-9-12-lo.statement: Demonstrate how perceptual reasoning at a higher level of abstraction draws upon earlier, lower levels of abstraction.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-b-iv-9-12-eu.statement: Scenes are composed of objects, which are composed of surfaces and boundaries. Boundaries are marked by contours, which are composed of edges, which are made up of pixels.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-c-i-k-2-lo.statement: Describe some things an intelligent agent must "know" in order to make sense of a question.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-c-i-k-2-eu.statement: To understand spoken requests, computers must know our vocabulary and pronunciation conventions, and they must be able to distinguish a question from a command.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-c-i-3-5-lo.statement: Demonstrate how a text to speech system can resolve ambiguity based on context, and how its error rate goes up when given ungrammatical or meaningless inputs.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-c-i-3-5-eu.statement: Speech recognition systems are trained on millions of utterances, allowing them to distinguish common from uncommon sequences of words, which helps them select the most likely interpretation of the signal.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-c-i-6-8-lo.statement: Classify a given image (e.g., "traffic scene", "nature scene", "social gathering", etc.) and then describe the kinds of knowledge a computer would need in order to understand scenes of this type.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-c-i-6-8-eu.statement: Domain knowledge for vision includes knowing what kinds of objects are likely to appear in a scene, where they are likely to appear in relation to other objects, and how occlusions and shadows can alter object appearances.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-c-i-9-12-lo.statement: Analyze one or more online image datasets and describe the information the datasets provide and how this can be used to extract domain knowledge for a computer vision system.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-c-i-9-12-eu.statement: Domain knowledge in AI systems is often derived from statistics collected from millions of sentences or images.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-c-ii-k-2-lo.statement: Discuss why intelligent agents need to be able to understand languages other than English.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-c-ii-k-2-eu.statement: Speech recognition systems need to accommodate different languages because many different types of people will use them.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-c-ii-3-5-lo.statement: Discuss how domain knowledge needs to be broad enough to encompass all the groups an application is intended to serve.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-c-ii-3-5-eu.statement: Speech recognition systems need to accommodate different types of accents and alternative pronunciations. Music recognition systems must know about different musical genres.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-c-ii-6-8-lo.statement: Describe how a vision system might exhibit cultural bias if it lacked knowledge of objects not found in the culture of the people who created it.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-c-ii-6-8-eu.statement: Domain knowledge must take multiple cultures into account if an AI application is to serve diverse groups.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-c-ii-9-12-lo.statement: Describe some of the technical difficulties in making computer perception systems function well for diverse groups.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-1-c-ii-9-12-eu.statement: Dark or low contrast facial features are harder to recognize than bright, high contrast features. Children's speech is in a higher register and less clearly articulated than adult speech.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-i-k-2-lo.statement: Construct a map of a home, school, or neighborhood.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-i-k-2-eu.statement: The map is not the territory. A map is a representation of a territory.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-i-3-5-lo.statement: Demonstrate how different styles of map capture different aspects of the world.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-i-3-5-eu.statement: Maps can be geometrically accurate or just show which places are reachable from which other places (topology). They can contain many types of information, such as the names and sizes of cities and towns, or the types of roads connecting them.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-i-6-8-lo.statement: Show how a game board (e.g., tic-tac-toe, Chutes and Ladders, Monopoly, chess) can be represented by a description in plain language.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-i-6-8-eu.statement: The essential information in a game board is the set of squares that make up the board, the relationships among those squares, and the positions of the pieces.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-i-9-12-lo.statement: Describe how to represent a concept as a schema.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-i-9-12-eu.statement: A schema describes a concept by listing its superconcepts and defining its properties, some of which may be inherited from superconcepts.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-ii-k-2-lo.statement: Give examples of symbols you encounter in daily life.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-ii-k-2-eu.statement: Concepts can be represented using symbols in place of words.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-ii-3-5-lo.statement: Give examples of tree structures commonly used by people and explain the relationships among the components.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-ii-3-5-eu.statement: Many types of information have a hierarchical structure, which can be visualized as a tree.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-ii-6-8-lo.statement: Illustrate translation of a structure such as a game board, road map, or mind map into a labeled graph and explain the contributions of the components.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-ii-6-8-eu.statement: The nodes of a graph represent things, and the links represent relationships between those things. Labels supply additional information about what the nodes and links represent.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-ii-9-12-lo.statement: Translate the premises of a syllogism expressed in English into logical notation and complete the syllogism correctly.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-ii-9-12-eu.statement: Syllogisms represent statements about categories and instances in a way that allows computers to derive new knowledge from existing knowledge by following simple inference rules.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-iii-k-2-lo.statement: Draw a tree by repeatedly splitting each branch into sub-branches multiple times, and putting a piece of data at each branch.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-iii-k-2-eu.statement: A tree is a way of organizing information.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-iii-3-5-lo.statement: Describe the parts of a tree and how those parts are related.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-iii-3-5-eu.statement: A tree is a collection of labeled nodes, each of which (save the root) has a link to a parent node above it in the hierarchy. Childless nodes are called leaves or terminal nodes; those with children are non-terminal nodes.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-iii-6-8-lo.statement: Describe the parts of a graph and how those parts are related.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-iii-6-8-eu.statement: A graph is a collection of labeled nodes connected by labeled links. Every link has a source node and a target node; every node has a set of incoming links and a set of outgoing links. Trees are a special case of graphs.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-iii-9-12-lo.statement: Describe how schemas are used to structure information about people, places, or things in knowledge graphs.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-iii-9-12-eu.statement: A schema specifies the attributes of the concept being described, and its relationships to other concepts, e.g., the Restaurant schema inherits properties from the FoodEstablishment schema.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-iv-k-2-lo.statement: Identify the features that make each object in a collection unique, and create a table of features to organize the objects.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-iv-k-2-eu.statement: Objects can be described in terms of the features they possess.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-iv-3-5-lo.statement: Construct a feature vector representation for a set of objects and show how similar objects are close together in feature space.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-iv-3-5-eu.statement: Recommender systems represent things like movies, books, consumer products, or social media posts using feature vectors.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-iv-6-8-lo.statement: Explain how word embeddings (which are feature vectors) represent words as sequences of numbers.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-iv-6-8-eu.statement: Word embeddings are a key part of neural natural language processing, including machine translation (e.g., Google Translate) and text generation systems (BERT, GPT3, etc.)

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-iv-9-12-lo.statement: Describe how a transformer network operates.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-a-iv-9-12-eu.statement: Transformer networks map sequences of input words to sequences of output words, where words are represented as feature vectors.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-b-i-k-2-lo.statement: Illustrate a next possible state in the game of tic-tac-toe given a starting state.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-b-i-k-2-eu.statement: A game such as tic-tac-toe can be described as a sequence of states, where each move transitions from a state to a successor state.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-b-i-3-5-lo.statement: Illustrate how a computer can represent the playing of a game such as tic-tac-toe or nim by drawing the linear sequence of board positions produced by the players' moves.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-b-i-3-5-eu.statement: Computers play games and solve puzzles by creating a sequence of states (board positions) connected by legal moves, using an algorithm to choose their next move at each step.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-b-i-6-8-lo.statement: Illustrate how a computer can solve a maze, find a route on a map, or reason about concepts in a knowledge graph by drawing a search tree.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-b-i-6-8-eu.statement: Computers solve mazes, find driving routes, and reason about concepts in knowledge graphs using graph search algorithms, which construct search trees.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-b-i-9-12-lo.statement: Identify types of real-world problems that are search problems and describe their states and operators.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-b-i-9-12-eu.statement: Computers can solve many types of problems using search techniques if the problem can be described in terms of finding a path from a start state to a goal state.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-b-ii-k-2-lo.statement: Draw a simple search tree to illustrate two possible choices of moves by drawing two different successor states to a given tic-tac-toe game board state, forming a tree.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-b-ii-k-2-eu.statement: A computer must make choices when playing games, in the same way that humans do.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-b-ii-3-5-lo.statement: Given a state of a game such as tic-tac-toe or nim, draw a search tree showing all possible next moves and their resulting states, and pick the best next move.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-b-ii-3-5-eu.statement: Computer game playing programs may construct search trees to decide on their next move.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-b-ii-6-8-lo.statement: Model the process of solving a graph search problem using breadth-first search to draw a search tree.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-b-ii-6-8-eu.statement: Breadth-first search can be used to solve problems that involve reasoning about graphs.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-b-ii-9-12-lo.statement: Illustrate breadth-first, depth-first, and best-first search algorithms to grow a search tree for a graph search problem.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-b-ii-9-12-eu.statement: There are multiple algorithms for generating a search tree, each with its own advantages.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-c-i-k-2-lo.statement: Identify problems as either classification problems or search problems.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-c-i-k-2-eu.statement: In classification problems we decide what kind of thing we have based on its features. In search problems we find a path from a start to a goal, such as finding a route on a map or exploring possible moves in a game.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-c-i-3-5-lo.statement: Categorize problems as either classification problems or search problems.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-c-i-3-5-eu.statement: Classification problems assign each input to one of a predetermined set of classes. Search problems construct answers by applying operators to states to generate new states.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-c-i-6-8-lo.statement: Categorize problems as classification, prediction, combinatorial search, or sequential decision problems.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-c-i-6-8-eu.statement: Prediction problems are similar to classification problems except they estimate a continuous value, such as height or daily temperature. Sequential decision problems choose the next move for any given state in order to maximize overall reward.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-c-i-9-12-lo.statement: Categorize real-world problems as classification, prediction, sequential decision problems, combinatorial search, heuristic search, adversarial search, logical deduction, or statistical inference.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-c-i-9-12-eu.statement: Reasoning problems can be categorized based on the types of inputs supplied, the types of outputs to be produced, and the characteristics of the search space, if applicable.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-c-ii-k-2-lo.statement: Model the use of a classification or search algorithm to solve a problem.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-c-ii-k-2-eu.statement: Reasoning algorithms are ways to solve reasoning problems.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-c-ii-3-5-lo.statement: Describe the differences between two algorithms for classifying things: decision trees, or neural networks like Teachable Machine.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-c-ii-3-5-eu.statement: Multiple algorithms can be used to solve a reasoning problem.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-c-ii-6-8-lo.statement: Compare several algorithms that could be used to solve a specific type of reasoning problem.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-c-ii-6-8-eu.statement: The choice of reasoning algorithm depends on the characteristics of the input data and the types of decisions to be made.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-c-ii-9-12-lo.statement: For each of these types of reasoning problems (classification, prediction, sequential decision making, combinatorial search, heuristic search, adversarial search, logical deduction, and statistical inference), list an algorithm that could be used to solve that problem.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-2-c-ii-9-12-eu.statement: AI includes a wide variety of reasoning algorithms for solving different types of reasoning problems. Some use symbolic representations (e.g., search trees) while others are numerical in nature (e.g., neural nets operating on feature vectors).

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-i-k-2-lo.statement: Describe and provide examples of how people learn and how computers learn.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-i-3-5-lo.statement: Differentiate between how people learn and how computers learn.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-i-3-5-eu.statement: Both people and computers can learn by finding patterns in data, or by trial and error. But people are flexible learners who can adapt to unfamiliar situations and learn in other ways, such as by observing others, by asking questions, or by making connections to prior learning.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-i-6-8-lo.statement: Contrast the unique characteristics of human learning with the ways machine learning systems operate.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-i-6-8-eu.statement: People learn by observation, by being told, by asking questions, by experimentation, by practice, and by making connections to past experience. Computers learn by applying specialized algorithms to large amounts of training data, or by thousands or even millions of trial and error experiences, to solve narrowly defined problems.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-i-9-12-lo.statement: Define supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning algorithms, and give examples of human learning that are similar to each algorithm.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-i-9-12-eu.statement: Both supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms find patterns in data. Supervised learning uses features to predict the class label supplied by a teacher; unsupervised learning groups similar instances together, creating its own classes. Reinforcement learning uses trial and error to find a policy for choosing actions that maximizes the reinforcement signal.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-ii.statement: Nature of Learning (Finding patterns in data)

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-ii-k-2-lo.statement: Identify patterns in labeled data and determine the features that predict labels.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-ii-k-2-eu.statement: Classes can be defined in terms of feature values. The relevant features can be inferred by examining labeled examples.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-ii-3-5-lo.statement: Model how supervised learning identifies patterns in labeled data.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-ii-3-5-eu.statement: When learning to classify labeled data, the patterns (or rules) that are discovered can be expressed as weights in a neural network or nodes in a decision tree.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-ii-6-8-lo.statement: Model how unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabeled data.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-ii-6-8-eu.statement: Unsupervised learning is useful when we don't know in advance what classes exist. It discovers patterns (or classes) in data by grouping nearby points into clusters.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-ii-9-12-lo.statement: Model how machine learning constructs a reasoner for classification or prediction by adjusting the reasoner's parameters (its internal representations).

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-ii-9-12-eu.statement: Supervised learning adjusts the parameters of a mathematical model (selected in advance by a human) to generate correct classifications or predictions.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-iii-k-2-lo.statement: Demonstrate how to train a computer to recognize something.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-iii-3-5-lo.statement: Train a classification model using machine learning, and then examine the accuracy of the model on new inputs.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-iii-3-5-eu.statement: Computers can learn to classify instances or predict values by being shown labeled examples. If the results on new inputs are unsatisfactory, additional training may be required to improve the accuracy.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-iii-6-8-lo.statement: Train and evaluate a classification or prediction model using machine learning on a tabular dataset.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-iii-6-8-eu.statement: Computers can learn to classify instances or predict values by examining feature values. If the results on new inputs are unsatisfactory, additional training may be required to improve the accuracy.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-iii-9-12-lo.statement: Use either a supervised or unsupervised learning algorithm to train a model on real world data, then evaluate the results.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-iii-9-12-eu.statement: In supervised learning the model is trained on a training set to produce the correct labels for labeled data. In unsupervised learning, the model is trained to assign each input to a cluster of similar inputs.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-iv.statement: Nature of Learning (Constructing vs. using a reasoner)

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-iv-3-5-lo.statement: Demonstrate how training data are labeled when using a machine learning tool.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-iv-3-5-eu.statement: In preparation for training a model, training data can be labeled by first defining the classes (the labels) and then adding examples for each class separately.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-iv-6-8-lo.statement: Explain the difference between training and using a reasoning model.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-iv-6-8-eu.statement: Machine learning algorithms use labeled training data to construct reasoning models that do classification or prediction. Once training is complete, the reasoning model can be applied to new data to solve problems or make decisions.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-iv-9-12-lo.statement: Illustrate what happens during each of the steps required when using machine learning to construct a classifier or predictor.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-iv-9-12-eu.statement: The steps are: deciding what problem you want to solve, figuring out where you will obtain the training data, choosing a feature set, figuring out how to label the data, running the learning algorithm, use of a cross-validation set to decide when training should stop, and using a test set to measure performance.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-v-3-5-lo.statement: Analyze a game where one constructs a decision tree, describing the organization of the tree and the learning algorithm used to add nodes.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-v-3-5-eu.statement: In a decision tree learning game, the tree's branch nodes are questions and the leaf nodes are classes.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-v-6-8-lo.statement: Compare how a decision tree learning algorithm works vs. how a neural network learning algorithm works.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-v-6-8-eu.statement: In decision tree learning, each step adds a new node, which tests a single feature value. In neural network learning, each step makes a small change to every weight in the network.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-v-9-12-lo.statement: Describe how various types of machine learning algorithms learn by adjusting their internal representations.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-v-9-12-eu.statement: Decision tree learners build decision trees by adding nodes one at a time. Neural net learning algorithms adjust weights. Regression algorithms adjust equation parameters. Reinforcement learners update value predictions or policies.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-vi-3-5-lo.statement: Explain how reinforcement learning allows a computer to learn from experience (i.e., trial and error).

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-vi-3-5-eu.statement: Computers can learn from experience if there is a "reinforcement" signal indicating whether the computer's actions are leading to good or bad outcomes.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-vi-6-8-lo.statement: Explain the differences between supervised learning and reinforcement learning.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-vi-6-8-eu.statement: Supervised learning tells the agent what output it should produce for each input; reinforcement learning only tells the agent how well it's doing as it chooses actions to take.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-vi-9-12-lo.statement: Select the appropriate type of machine learning algorithm (supervised, unsupervised, or reinforcement learning) to solve a reasoning problem.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-a-vi-9-12-eu.statement: Major types of learning algorithms and the kinds of reasoning problems they are used to solve are: supervised learning, used for classification and prediction; unsupervised learning, used for clustering; and reinforcement learning, used for sequential decision making.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-b-i.statement: Neural Networks (Structure of a neural network)

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-b-i-3-5-lo.statement: Illustrate how a neural network of 1 to 3 neurons is a function that computes an output.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-b-i-3-5-eu.statement: A neural network uses one or more neurons working together to form a function. Each neuron takes a set of numbers as input and produces a single number as its output.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-b-i-6-8-lo.statement: Illustrate the structure of a neural network and describe how its parts form a set of functions that compute an output.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-b-i-6-8-eu.statement: Neural networks are organized as layers of units (input, hidden, and output layers), with weighted connections between units in successive layers.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-b-i-9-12-lo.statement: Describe the following neural network architectures and their uses: feed-forward network, 2D convolutional network, recurrent network, generative adversarial network.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-b-i-9-12-eu.statement: Feed-forward networks can learn arbitrary functions and are used for both classification and regression. 2D convolutional networks are used for image analysis. Recurrent networks are used for language processing. Generative adversarial networks are used to create deepfakes.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-b-ii-3-5-lo.statement: Demonstrate how weights are assigned in a neural network to produce a desired input/output behavior.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-b-ii-3-5-eu.statement: The behavior of a neural network can be altered by adjusting its weights.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-b-ii-6-8-lo.statement: Demonstrate how a learning rule can be used to adjust the weights in a one-layer neural network.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-b-ii-6-8-eu.statement: During training, weights are adjusted in response to errors in the network's output, so that an error will be less likely when the input is seen again.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-b-ii-9-12-lo.statement: Train a multilayer neural network using the backpropagation learning algorithm and describe how the weights of the neurons and the outputs of the hidden units change as a result of learning.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-b-ii-9-12-eu.statement: A neuron's weights start out as small random values and evolve to a more precise pattern through learning. The changes in the neuron's weights are computed by a learning rule driven by a back-propagated error signal.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-i-k-2-lo.statement: Create a labeled dataset with explicit features to illustrate how computers can learn to classify things like foods, movies, or toys.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-i-k-2-eu.statement: We can get a computer to classify things by describing them in terms of feature values the computer can reason about. People choose the features.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-i-3-5-lo.statement: Create a labeled dataset with explicit features of several types and use a machine learning tool to train a classifier on this data.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-i-3-5-eu.statement: Feature types include discrete values (e.g., "New York", "Pennsylvania", "Iowa"), binary values (yes/no), and continuous values (age, height).

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-i-6-8-lo.statement: Create a dataset for training a decision tree classifier or predictor and explore the impact that different feature encodings have on the decision tree.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-i-6-8-eu.statement: The choice of features to include, and the best encoding to use for these features, depends on the particular reasoning problem we are trying to solve.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-i-9-12-lo.statement: Compare two real world datasets in terms of the features they comprise and how those features are encoded.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-i-9-12-eu.statement: Humans decide which features to include in a dataset and how to encode them. This can have consequences for machine learning algorithms trained on these datasets.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-ii-3-5-lo.statement: Illustrate how training a classifier for a broad concept such as "dog" requires a large amount of data to capture the diversity of the domain.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-ii-3-5-eu.statement: Machine learning requires large amounts of data to be effective. To recognize dogs in images one must have not only many types of dogs, but also many different viewing angles and contexts.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-ii-6-8-lo.statement: Illustrate how objects in an image can be segmented and labeled to construct a training set for object recognition.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-ii-6-8-eu.statement: Machine learning requires large amounts of data to be effective. Human expertise is usually required to label the data, which could be labor intensive.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-ii-9-12-lo.statement: Evaluate a dataset used to train a real AI system by considering the size of the dataset, the way that the data were acquired and labeled, the storage required, and the estimated time to produce the dataset.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-ii-9-12-eu.statement: A large dataset is typically required to capture the diversity of a complex domain and narrow down the range of possible reasoner behaviors. Labeling training data is labor-intensive and may require specialized expertise. Bias can be introduced during each step of dataset creation.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-iii-k-2-lo.statement: Examine a labeled dataset and identify problems in the data that could lead a computer to make incorrect predictions.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-iii-k-2-eu.statement: How well a computer learns to classify depends on the data used to train it.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-iii-3-5-lo.statement: Examine features and labels of training data to detect potential sources of bias.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-iii-3-5-eu.statement: Machine learning algorithms require a representative collection of data in order to build an accurate model. Training datasets drawn from historical data may reflect pre-existing human and societal biases.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-iii-6-8-lo.statement: Explain how the choice of training data shapes the behavior of the classifier, and how bias can be introduced if the training set is not properly balanced.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-iii-6-8-eu.statement: Bias can result if the model is asked to classify inputs that don't resemble the training data, or if the training data contains irrelevant correlations we don't want the classifier to rely on.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-iii-9-12-lo.statement: Investigate imbalances in training data in terms of gender, age, ethnicity, or other demographic variables that could result in a biased model, by using a data visualization tool.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-3-c-iii-9-12-eu.statement: Machine learning algorithms will take advantage of any imbalances or correlations in the training set that help lower the error rate. If the dataset is not representative, those correlations can be misleading.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-i-k-2-lo.statement: Demonstrate knowledge of the structure of language through tasks such as generating plausible and implausible novel words, or reordering the words in a scrambled sentence so that it makes sense.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-i-k-2-eu.statement: Human languages have rules for how words and sentences are constructed, and computers can use these rules to help them figure out what people are saying.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-i-3-5-lo.statement: Demonstrate that human language is infinite by showing how any sentence can be repeatedly extended to form a more complex sentence.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-i-3-5-eu.statement: Human language can express an infinite number of ideas and form an infinite number of sentences. This property makes it impossible to pre-program a computer with a response to every sentence.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-i-6-8-lo.statement: Demonstrate a computer's grasp of grammar by using a parser program to display the syntactic structure of a sentence, and explain what the nodes represent.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-i-6-8-eu.statement: Parse trees are a way of representing the syntactic structure of a sentence, showing the relationships between words. Computers can use syntax trees to both analyze and generate sentences.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-i-9-12-lo.statement: Identify portions of a text that would be difficult for a computer to understand, and explain why.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-i-9-12-eu.statement: Computers have difficulty understanding text that makes use of metaphor, imagery, hyperbole, sarcasm, or humor, or word play.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-ii-k-2-lo.statement: Illustrate the ambiguity of language by giving examples of homophones and homonyms and showing how the correct word can be determined using context.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-ii-k-2-eu.statement: Different words may sound the same, but people and computers can use the surrounding words to determine the correct one.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-ii-3-5-lo.statement: Illustrate how understanding a sentence could be challenging for a computer by giving sentences where a pronoun could refer to either of two nouns.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-ii-3-5-eu.statement: Sentences can have multiple meanings depending on which noun a pronoun is thought to be referencing. People and (to a lesser extent) computers can use context and world knowledge to select the most likely meaning.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-ii-6-8-lo.statement: Illustrate how understanding a sentence could be challenging for a computer by giving sentences where a prepositional phrase could attach in either of two places, and show how this ambiguity can sometimes be resolved based on meaning.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-ii-6-8-eu.statement: Language is often ambiguous, but some possible meanings can be ruled out if they don't make sense. Computers are not yet as good as people at using context and world knowledge to make these judgments.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-ii-9-12-lo.statement: Illustrate how understanding a sentence could be challenging for a computer by describing multiple senses of a given word.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-ii-9-12-eu.statement: A single word can have multiple senses. People use context and world knowledge to determine the correct sense, but computers don't typically represent meaning with this degree of subtlety.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-iii-k-2-lo.statement: Demonstrate how a computer can produce different forms of a verb, such as present or past tense.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-iii-k-2-eu.statement: In order for a computer to speak naturally with humans it must be able to understand how words are constructed and put words in the proper form.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-iii-3-5-lo.statement: Experiment with a speech to text system to see if it resolves alternative word choices correctly based on context.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-iii-3-5-eu.statement: Speech recognition systems can use grammar and context to resolve ambiguous words but they don't always get it right.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-iii-6-8-lo.statement: Illustrate how word embeddings can be used to reason about the meaning of words.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-iii-6-8-eu.statement: Word embeddings represent words with similar meanings as nearby points in a semantic feature space, and allow us to reason about words by doing arithmetic.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-iii-9-12-lo.statement: Demonstrate how a small context-free grammar can be used to parse or generate simple sentences.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-iii-9-12-eu.statement: Context-free grammars describe how words are combined into phrases and clauses, and can represent much of the syntactic structure of natural language, but don't handle things like subject-verb agreement well.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-iv-k-2-lo.statement: Demonstrate the kinds of tasks an intelligent assistant can and cannot perform.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-iv-k-2-eu.statement: Intelligent assistants (e.g., Siri, Alexa) are computers designed to respond to a limited set of requests. They cannot engage in a conversation like a human.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-iv-3-5-lo.statement: Demonstrate some types of questions that a search engine or intelligent assistant can answer, and some types that it cannot answer.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-iv-3-5-eu.statement: Search engines (e.g., Google) and intelligent assistants (e.g., Siri, Alexa) have a collection of specialized and general purpose modules they draw upon to answer different types of questions.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-iv-6-8-lo.statement: Describe some NLP (Natural Language Processing) tasks computers can perform, and explain how they work.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-iv-6-8-eu.statement: NLP tasks include text summarization, text generation, sentiment analysis, question answering, machine translation, and conversational interaction.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-iv-9-12-lo.statement: Describe several approaches to Natural Language Processing, ranging from simple to more sophisticated.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-a-iv-9-12-eu.statement: Simple NLP approaches include keyword matching, dictionary lookup, and template matching, while newer, more sophisticated but less transparent approaches use deep neural networks and machine learning.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-b-i-k-2-lo.statement: Give commonsense explanations of human behavior or events that might be useful for a robot to know.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-b-i-k-2-eu.statement: Choosing the most likely ending for a story is an example of commonsense reasoning, which requires knowledge about people and things, and how they behave, that computers may not have.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-b-i-3-5-lo.statement: Explain what knowledge would be required for a computer to understand a story.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-b-i-3-5-eu.statement: AI has trouble understanding stories because it doesn't have the knowledge that humans have about everyday life.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-b-i-6-8-lo.statement: Explain the knowledge a computer would need to solve a naive physics reasoning problem.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-b-i-6-8-eu.statement: Computers can reason about physical phenomena using naive physics inference rules, which formalize our intuitive understanding of concepts such as mass, volume, forces, and motion. At present, computers are not very good at this.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-b-i-9-12-lo.statement: Explain the cultural and naive physics knowledge required for a computer to correctly interpret a fable or fairytale.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-b-i-9-12-eu.statement: For humans or computers to infer the meaning of a story requires understanding of cultural knowledge, naive physics, and folk psychology. This is still difficult for computers.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-c-i-k-2-lo.statement: Demonstrate how computers recognize emotions in faces.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-c-i-k-2-eu.statement: Computers recognize emotions in faces by looking at the shapes of the mouth, eyes, and eyebrows.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-c-i-3-5-lo.statement: Illustrate how computers can judge the emotional tone of text.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-c-i-3-5-eu.statement: Computers can recognize positive and negative statements about a topic using natural language processing techniques known as "sentiment analysis".

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-c-i-6-8-lo.statement: Describe how computers use different types of cues to recognize human emotional states.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-c-i-6-8-eu.statement: Computers can recognize human emotional states by looking at facial expressions, gaze, gestures, body language, tone of voice, and choice of words.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-c-i-9-12-lo.statement: Identify ways AI applications can modify their behavior to respond to people's emotional states.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-c-i-9-12-eu.statement: Computers can respond appropriately to human emotions by acknowledging what the human is feeling and responding in a way that the human finds supportive and socially appropriate.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-d-i-k-2-lo.statement: Demonstrate some ways that intelligent agents don't understand things the way people do.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-d-i-k-2-eu.statement: Artificial Intelligence devices are not people, they are computer programs designed by people.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-d-i-3-5-lo.statement: Demonstrate what a broad AI system could do that current narrow AI systems cannot do.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-d-i-3-5-eu.statement: "Narrow AI" has given us a collection of algorithms that are good at specific things. "Broad AI" or "General AI" promises to give us general reasoning ability comparable to a human.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-d-i-6-8-lo.statement: Define criteria for consciousness and evaluate AI systems or fictional AI characters according to those criteria.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-d-i-6-8-eu.statement: The nature of consciousness is an unsolved problem, but two important criteria seem to be self-awareness and personal history.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-d-i-9-12-lo.statement: Debate alternative perspectives on human vs. artificial intelligence.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-4-d-i-9-12-eu.statement: Some AI experts and philosophers have argued that computers can never achieve fully human-like intelligence, while others believe that AI will eventually exceed human intelligence.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-i.statement: Ethical AI (Diversity of Interests and Disparate Impacts)

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-i-k-2-lo.statement: Evaluate the ways a decision impacts people differently.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-i-k-2-eu.statement: Computers can sometimes make a decision that works for most people but harms or disadvantages other people.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-i-3-5-lo.statement: Evaluate how an AI technology can have different effects on different groups of people.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-i-3-5-eu.statement: The decisions made when developing an AI system can impact different people and communities in different ways.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-i-6-8-lo.statement: Evaluate the ways various stakeholders' goals and values influence the design of AI systems.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-i-6-8-eu.statement: The behavior of AI systems is determined by the choices of the designers, which may involve tradeoffs between conflicting goals and values.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-i-9-12-lo.statement: Explain how use of AI systems has led to disparate impacts on different groups.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-i-9-12-eu.statement: Different groups of people may be affected differently by AI systems.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-ii-k-2-lo.statement: Discuss the characteristics of systems that are fair and unfair and the impact on people when a system is not fair.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-ii-k-2-eu.statement: AI systems should be designed to benefit people. Creators of these systems should make sure that their systems treat everyone fairly.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-ii-3-5-lo.statement: Evaluate how an AI system meets the design criteria of transparency and explainability.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-ii-3-5-eu.statement: An AI system is transparent if we know what data and decision making criteria it uses. Part of transparency is having the system provide explanations for its decisions.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-ii-6-8-lo.statement: Evaluate how an AI system meets the design criteria of accountability and respect for privacy.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-ii-6-8-eu.statement: Accountability in AI systems means designers and decision makers take responsibility for the system's actions. Respect for privacy means the system does not act in ways that violate people's privacy rights.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-ii-9-12-lo.statement: Analyze an AI system to determine whether it satisfies ethical design criteria.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-ii-9-12-eu.statement: To ensure that AI systems are helpful and not harmful, ethical design criteria include: fairness, transparency, explainability, accountability, respect for privacy, and adherence to societal values.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-iii-3-5-lo.statement: Create a model card for a classification or prediction model.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-iii-3-5-eu.statement: Model cards support transparency by explaining the intended use, training dataset, accuracy, and limitations of the model.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-iii-6-8-lo.statement: Evaluate ways that AI system designers can learn about and incorporate the values of their stakeholders into the design process.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-iii-6-8-eu.statement: AI systems need to align with the norms and values of the groups they aim to serve. Developers of AI systems need to understand that values vary across cultures.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-iii-9-12-lo.statement: Design an AI System using an ethical design process.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-a-iii-9-12-eu.statement: Ethical design, at all stages of the design process, considers the values of all stakeholders and upholds the principles of fairness, transparency, explainability, accountability, respect for privacy, and adherence to societal values.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-b-i-k-2-lo.statement: Identify devices in daily life that use AI technologies.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-b-i-k-2-eu.statement: AI technologies are part of any device that includes speech recognition or computer vision, such as smart phones, intelligent home assistants, and modern automobiles.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-b-i-3-5-lo.statement: Describe how AI-powered services are used in daily life.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-b-i-3-5-eu.statement: AI-powered services are used to look up information, to provide voice interfaces to many kinds of apps, to make recommendations based on a person's interests, and to make cars safer.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-b-i-6-8-lo.statement: Examine an aspect of daily life that is predicted to change due to the introduction of AI technologies.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-b-i-6-8-eu.statement: AI technologies are changing daily life as intelligent machines find new roles in society.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-b-i-9-12-lo.statement: Explain the kinds of debates that might arise as AI technology continues to evolve and is further woven into our culture.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-b-i-9-12-eu.statement: Some new AI technologies will pose challenges for cultural norms and expectations that society must identify and wrestle with.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-b-ii-3-5-lo.statement: Analyze deepfake images or videos and identify the flaws that reveal them as deepfakes.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-b-ii-3-5-eu.statement: Current deepfakes have detectable flaws, but as the technology improves it will undermine our trust in digital media.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-b-ii-6-8-lo.statement: Critique uses of AI technology that can be used to surveil people or violate their privacy.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-b-ii-6-8-eu.statement: AI technologies endanger privacy by reducing the cost of implementing widespread surveillance and enabling new types of surveillance.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-b-ii-9-12-lo.statement: Identify areas where it is appropriate to regulate use of AI technologies and evaluate regulations that have been proposed.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-b-ii-9-12-eu.statement: Legal regulation of AI technologies is appropriate in areas where there are societal values that require protection.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-c-i.statement: AI & the Economy (Impacts of AI on Sectors of Society)

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-c-i-k-2-lo.statement: Identify current uses of AI and how they have impacted society.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-c-i-k-2-eu.statement: Society has undergone changes because of AI and this will continue in the future.

OE-COMPETENCY-ai4k12-5-c-i-3-5-lo.statement: Identify changes in how sectors of society operate due to the introduction of AI.
