comp.focusRule: Aligned only where a stage's technical content (representation, data, search, models, training, datasets, program behaviour) meets an AI4K12 item a teacher could defend. Weak matches are marked weak. Societal, ethical and cognitive items were left to the Interdisciplinary space. Where an item has a technical core, I aligned on that core and said so in senseDiffers. Stages with no counterpart got none.

items.why: The stage has children say what an arrow, icon or letter stands for. The item asks for examples of symbols met in daily life. Both treat a symbol as something that stands for an idea.
The stage sorts objects by one property and names it. The item asks children to find what makes each object unique and to tabulate it. Only the idea of describing objects by what they have is shared.
items.senseDiffers: AI4K12 features are values a computer can reason about. The stage says property and sorts by one at a time. It builds no feature table.

items.why: The stage has children label each group with a word or picture. The item has children create a labelled dataset with features. Labelling groups is a first step toward a labelled dataset, but the stage builds no dataset for a computer.
items.senseDiffers: In AI4K12 a label is a class name that a computer learns to predict. In the stage a label names a group that a child made.

items.why: The stage asks what a chart leaves out. The item has children show how different map styles capture different aspects of the world. Both teach that a representation keeps some things and drops others. The stage compares no styles.
items.senseDiffers: The item is about maps of places. The stage is about charts of measured data, a different kind of representation.

items.why: The stage records measurements in a table. The item builds a row of values for each object and compares objects by closeness. The table is the same structure. The stage does not compare closeness.

No 6-8 item covers image encoding. The 3-5 item asks how an image is stored as numbers. The stage encodes a small image in binary with a stated scheme, so it covers the item and adds text and a comparison of encodings.

The item asks how sound becomes numbers by sampling. The stage has no sound and names no sampling rate. The shared idea is that media are stored as numbers, which the stage teaches for text and images.
items.senseDiffers: AI4K12 files encoding under sensing, as the way a machine takes in the world. The stage treats encoding as a scheme chosen for stored data.

items.why: The item says the best encoding of features depends on the problem. The stage compares two encodings of the same data on size and kept detail. Both show that an encoding choice changes what can be done with the data.
items.senseDiffers: In AI4K12 encoding means how a feature value is written for a classifier. In the stage it means a binary scheme for text, an image or numbers.

items.why: The item says people decide which features go into a dataset and how to encode them, with consequences downstream. The stage names a limit of a representation and its effect on a result. The overlap is the effect of an encoding choice.
items.senseDiffers: The item concerns features in a machine learning dataset. The stage concerns limits such as precision or size in any representation. AI4K12 has no item on information in bits or compression.

stageAlignments.none: AI4K12 has no item on following or writing steps. Its algorithm items start from reasoning and learning algorithms. Writing and fixing steps belongs to general computing standards, which this alignment does not cover.

items.why: The item draws the sequence of board positions a game produces. The stage traces the values a program stores at each step. Both follow how the stored condition of a system changes step by step.
items.senseDiffers: In the item, state is a board position in a game. The stage uses state for any values a program stores.

stageAlignments.none: The reviewer found no defensible AI4K12 match for this stage. The item asks for training and evaluating a model on a table of data. The stage has no data, model or training. Test cases against a specification and

items.why: The item says several algorithms can build a search tree, each with its own advantages. The stage compares algorithms for any task on step counts and names no search task. Both weigh one algorithm against another.
items.senseDiffers: AI4K12 algorithms here build search trees over states. The stage compares any algorithms on how steps grow with input. Search through a list would be a different sense of search.

items.why: The item says different reasoning problems call for different algorithms. The stage chooses between algorithms for a stated need and justifies the choice. Both tie the choice of algorithm to the problem.
items.senseDiffers: AI4K12 reasoning algorithms solve classification, search or inference problems. The stage compares algorithms for any task on how many steps they take.

items.why: The stage has children say who wrote a machine's rules and show a machine doing exactly what its instructions say. That meets the clause that AI devices are programs designed by people. The stage does not address the clause about people.
items.senseDiffers: The item sits under philosophy of mind. The alignment rests on the technical core only: a device runs a program that people wrote. The stage says nothing about understanding or about AI devices in particular.

items.why: The item says intelligent assistants respond to a limited set of requests. The stage asks for a machine doing exactly what its instructions say and what happens when they are wrong. Both tie a machine's behaviour to how it was set up.
items.senseDiffers: Technical core only: a device answers only the requests its program was built for. Intelligent in the item names a class of devices. The stage avoids the word.

items.why: The stage has children build a model with named parts and say one thing it leaves out. The item shows that different map styles capture different aspects. Both teach that a representation keeps some things and drops others. The stage compares no styles.
items.senseDiffers: The item is about maps of places. The stage's model is something that can be run and observed over time.

items.why: The item draws the sequence of states a game goes through. The stage runs a simulation and records what happens over time. Both follow a system through a sequence of states. The item uses game boards. The stage uses a pond or a queue.

The item says weights change in response to errors in the output. The stage identifies a feedback loop in a model. The error signal in training is one case of output returned to change later behaviour. The stage has no training or weights.
items.senseDiffers: In the item, feedback is an error signal used at each training step. In the stage the loop runs inside the model as agents act and the pattern changes.

items.why: The stage describes how machine learning adjusts parameters from data to improve a measured result. The item models how a reasoner is built by adjusting its parameters. The matching enduring understanding adds that a person selects the model in advance.
items.senseDiffers: AI4K12 speaks of learning and a reasoner. The stage keeps both as a parameter-adjusting procedure and attributes no understanding to the machine.

items.why: The item says search solves problems written as a path from a start state to a goal state. The stage names search on an objective as one of three methods to compare. Problem formulation, the item's content, is absent from the stage.
items.senseDiffers: The item's search finds a path of states to a goal. The stage's search explores candidates and keeps those that score higher on an objective, so it also covers optimisation.

items.why: The item sorts reasoning problems by input, output and search space. The stage compares three kinds of system on what each needs as input and what each guarantees. Both ask what goes in and what comes out. They sort different things.
items.senseDiffers: AI4K12 sorts problems such as classification, prediction and search. The stage sorts kinds of system: machine learning, search and distributed systems. Distributed systems have no AI4K12 counterpart.

items.why: The item says supervised and unsupervised learning find patterns in data and reinforcement learning uses trial and error. The stage describes machine learning as parameter adjustment from data. It does not separate the three kinds of learning.
items.senseDiffers: The item compares machine learning with human learning. The stage describes only the machine procedure and attributes no intention. The alignment rests on the machine side.

conceptAlignments.why: AI4K12 handles data in its Datasets rows: feature sets for training and large training sets. Computational-Core's Data is wider. It covers any recorded values that stand for something, from sorted objects to charted measurements.

Computational-Core's Representation names any structure that stands for something and can be stored or processed. In principle that includes the five AI4K12 rows. The stages teach only symbols, tables, charts and binary encodings.

Only the Representation (Abstraction) row matches: a map keeps some aspects and drops others, which is hiding detail. The two pipeline rows use abstraction for levels of processing from signal to meaning, which is a different sense.
AI4K12 names reasoning algorithms and search algorithms. Computational-Core's Algorithm is any finite sequence of steps that turns input into output, so these two are special cases.
AI4K12 uses state for a game position or a step in a search. Computational-Core's State is the stored values of any system at one moment, which includes a game position.

AI4K12 uses model for a trained mapping from inputs to outputs. Computational-Core's Model is a simplified description of a system that is run to see what follows. The senses meet where a trained model is run on new inputs.

AI4K12 search finds a path from a start state to a goal by growing a search tree. Computational-Core's Search explores candidates and keeps those that score higher on an objective. The two overlap on exploring options.

These AI4K12 rows cover finding patterns, training, using a trained model, adjusting internal representations, learning from experience and weight adjustment. Computational-Core's Machine Learning, a procedure that adjusts parameters from data to improve a result, is the general idea behind them.

Error signals and reinforcement signals are fed back to change later behaviour, so they are cases of feedback. In training the signal goes to the learning rule. In Computational-Core output is returned as input. AI4K12 has no row on feedback loops in models.

ai4k12Unaligned.why: Sound stored as samples of a waveform. C1:6-8 encodes text and images and could add sampling a sound into a series of numbers.
Simulating an edge detector on pixels. C1:6-8 or C2:6-8 could add a small program that finds features in an image from pixel values.
Trees as labelled nodes with parent links. No stage teaches tree structures. C1:3-5 could grow to cover them as a way to organise data.
Graphs as labelled nodes and links. No stage covers graphs. C1:6-8 could add them as a representation next to encodings.

Embeddings are numbers chosen so that words of similar meaning sit close together. C1:6-8 encodes text as character codes, which carry no meaning. A further encoding could show the difference between the two.
Statements written in logical notation so that a program derives new facts by inference rules. C1:9-12 or C2:9-12 could add rule-based derivation.
Schemas that list attributes and inherited properties, used in knowledge graphs. C1:9-12 could add structured records with inheritance as a data representation.
Graph search for mazes and routes builds a search tree. Search appears only at C3:9-12. C2:6-8 or C3:6-8 could add a small search program.
Drawing every possible next move in a simple game and picking the best. C2:3-5 or C3:3-5 could add this as a program that explores options.
Sorting problems into classification and search problems. C3:3-5 could add this when it compares what systems do with data.
Prediction and sequential decision problems alongside classification and search. C3:6-8 could add a way to name the kind of task a model performs.
Comparing a decision tree with a neural network as two ways to classify. Computational-Core compares methods only at C3:9-12.
Modelling how supervised learning finds patterns in labelled data. Machine learning enters Computational-Core only at C3:9-12. C3:3-5 or C3:6-8 could add a hands-on version.
Unsupervised learning groups nearby points into clusters. No stage covers clustering. C3:6-8 could add it next to feedback models.
Training a classifier and checking its accuracy on new inputs. No stage below C3:9-12 trains a model.
Training and evaluating a model on a tabular dataset. It connects to the C1 data tables. C3:6-8 could grow to cover it.
Training builds a reasoning model and using it applies the model to new data. Computational-Core does not yet separate these two phases.
Decision tree learning adds nodes and neural network learning changes weights. C3:9-12 mentions adjusting parameters but names no specific method.
A reinforcement signal lets a computer learn from trial and error. No stage covers a reward signal. C3:3-5 or C3:6-8 could connect it to Feedback.
Neural networks as layers of units with weighted connections. No stage describes this structure. C3:6-8 or C3:9-12 could add it as one model structure.
Machine learning needs large amounts of labelled data, and labelling takes labour. Technical need for data only. C3:9-12 could state it as a condition of Machine Learning.
Technical core only: a model misbehaves on inputs unlike its training data or when the data hold irrelevant correlations. C3:9-12 could state this as a limit of Machine Learning.
Technical core only: how well a computer classifies depends on its training data. Machine learning enters Computational-Core at C3:9-12, so an earlier stage would first need a classifier example.

Technical core only: simple methods such as keyword and template matching compared with learned methods on what each can guarantee. C2:9-12 or C3:9-12 could host the comparison with language as the example.

Steps of building a classifier: source the data, choose features, label, run learning, stop on a validation set, measure on a test set. C3:9-12 says what machine learning is and teaches no build or check steps.
Breadth-first, depth-first and best-first search growing a search tree. C3:9-12 names Search and teaches no search method. Best-first search scores candidates, which fits the space's own definition.

Train a model on data and evaluate the result. C3:9-12 describes parameter adjustment and has no indicator for training or evaluating. Covers the evaluation idea that the dropped C2:6-8 match claimed.

Technical core only: learning algorithms exploit imbalances and correlations in the training set, and an unrepresentative set makes those correlations misleading. C3:9-12 states no data limit of machine learning.

int.focusRule: I looked for a match across all five Big Ideas, using each stage's performance indicators and the domain senses of its concepts. Where a shared word differs in meaning (learning, agency, search), I matched on what students do and stated the difference. Stages on heredity, copying and selection in populations have no AI4K12 counterpart, so they received none.

items.why: The stage lists signs among the ways people share ideas. The item asks for symbols met in daily life. Signs are a kind of symbol, so the two share one example and little else.
items.senseDiffers: Both treat a sign or symbol as a stand-in. The stage frames signs as a way to tell others something. The item frames a symbol as replacing a word, with no computer use stated at this band.

stageAlignments.none: The stage compares communities, cooperation, conflict and the history of a tool. No 3-5 AI4K12 item asks for any of these. The 3-5 items on effects on different groups assume an AI technology the stage never introduces.

items.why: The stage separates norms from institutions and treats culture as transmitted practice. The item says AI must fit the norms and values of the groups it serves. Norms are the shared topic. The stage has no content on values across cultures or on AI design.
items.senseDiffers: In the stage, norms are informal expectations that students tell apart from institutions. In AI4K12, norms and values are requirements a designer must learn about, and 'values' means what stakeholders want.

items.why: The stage has students explain how technology and cultural selection shape an information environment such as a social media platform. The item says new AI technologies challenge cultural norms and expectations. A platform case could serve both.
items.senseDiffers: AI4K12 asks which norms are challenged and what debates follow. The stage asks for mechanisms: how a group-level outcome emerges and how a platform and its users shape each other.

items.why: The stage's third indicator has children see that acting to meet a need does not require thinking as a person does. The item has them show ways intelligent agents do not understand as people do. Both separate action from human-style understanding.
items.senseDiffers: The stage applies this to animals acting on their own needs. AI4K12 applies it to programs designed by people. An 'agent' in AI4K12 has goals set by a designer.

items.why: The stage asks for an animal or person learning a behavior by watching another. The item says people learn by observing others and by linking to earlier learning, while computers learn from data or trial and error. The stage covers the living half.
items.senseDiffers: The stage's learning is a lasting change in behavior from experience, in a living thing. A computer's learning adjusts numbers from example data and implies no understanding. Teaching and scaffolding have no machine counterpart here.

items.why: The stage defines agency without conscious intention. The item names self-awareness and personal history as criteria for consciousness in AI. The shared topic is awareness versus goal-directed behavior. The stage teaches no consciousness criteria and names no machine.
items.senseDiffers: The stage's agency applies to organisms and needs no consciousness. The item asks whether machines are conscious and calls the question unsolved. Agency and consciousness are different things in both.

items.why: The stage ranks four organisms on an agency spectrum and analyzes one designed system. The item has students debate human versus artificial intelligence. The shared topic is how machine systems compare with living ones. The stage sets up no debate.
items.senseDiffers: The stage grades agency as a capacity to act toward goals, with designer-set goals for software. The item debates whether machines can match human-like intelligence, which is a different question.

items.why: The stage has children explain an action by what the person wanted, such as reaching for a cup because of thirst. The item asks for commonsense explanations of human behavior. The stage covers the explaining. The item adds what a robot would need.
items.senseDiffers: AI4K12 frames commonsense as knowledge a computer may lack. The stage treats explaining by wants as a natural early skill in children.

items.why: In the guess-my-rule game, children test a hidden pattern with yes or no answers. The item asks students to model how supervised learning finds a pattern in labeled data. Both infer a rule from labeled examples. The stage models no machine process.
items.senseDiffers: Children choose their own test examples and reflect on whether they tried to confirm or refute a guess. A supervised learner fits the labeled data it is given. It does not choose examples or judge its own method.

items.why: The stage compares starting from a random guess with starting from the closest known example, then making small revisions. The item draws a search tree for a maze or route. Both concern moving through candidate solutions. The stage defines no states or operators.
items.senseDiffers: The stage describes a human habit, local search from a familiar start, with no fixed list of options. The item uses systematic graph search over defined states. One word, 'search', covers two procedures.

items.why: The stage explains that a search for a solution can test only ideas already generated. The full space of possible ideas stays untested. The item has students describe problems as search with states and operators. Both rest on a space of options.
items.senseDiffers: The stage uses search loosely for how people and science explore ideas, where the space is never fully listed. The item needs explicit states, operators and a goal, so the space is defined.

items.why: The stage has children notice that members of a family differ. The item has them identify the features that make each object unique and tabulate them. A table of how family members differ would meet both.
items.senseDiffers: In the stage, variation matters because some differences are passed on. The item lists features to describe or classify objects and has no idea of passing on.

stageAlignments.none: The stage compares passing on genes with passing on game rules, with change along the way. No 3-5 AI4K12 item covers inheritance, copying or change across generations. The nearest items concern one learner trained on data.

The stage covers variation, selection and transmission in biology and culture. AI4K12 has no item on variants being kept or dropped across rounds. Its learning items adjust one model, which is a different process from selection in a population.

items.why: The stage compares biological selection with algorithmic selection such as a genetic algorithm's fitness function. The item describes how machine learning methods improve by adjusting internal representations. Both are machine procedures that improve a score.
items.senseDiffers: Selection works on a population of candidates over rounds. The item's methods adjust one model's numbers or tree. AI4K12 does not name evolutionary algorithms, so the match covers only the improve-a-score idea.

conceptAlignments.why: Representation here spans mental, cultural, educational and computational stand-ins. AI4K12 covers the last two ends: maps, symbols, trees, graphs and feature vectors. Its rows say nothing about mental representation.
The education sense of Abstraction runs from drawing a map to describing a game board by its essential parts. AI4K12 row 2-A-i follows the same progression, from a map to a game board to a schema.

The AI sense of Model is a runnable description whose numbers were set from data. The AI4K12 rows on training a model, and on training versus using one, cover that sense. The scientific, cultural and cognitive senses have no row.

Learning here spans cognition, biology, culture, education and machine learning. AI4K12 rows on humans versus machines, finding patterns and learning from experience cover the machine sense and its contrast with people.
Search here has senses in computing, cognition, biology (foraging) and education. AI4K12 rows on state spaces and combinatorial search cover the computing sense only.

Algorithm here is a fixed series of steps, with senses in computation, education and technology. AI4K12 row 2-C-ii covers reasoning algorithms for classification and search, which is the computation sense.

The AI sense of Feedback is a training loop that compares output with a target or reward and adjusts numbers. AI4K12 rows on weight adjustment and on reinforcement signals cover it. The body-regulation and classroom senses have no row.
The AI sense of Incentive is a reward signal that a learning program collects more of. AI4K12 row 3-A-vi covers learning from a reinforcement signal. Prices, grades and animal payoffs have no row.

Information here is a pattern a receiver can use. AI4K12 covers how measurements are encoded as numbers and how perception extracts meaning from sensory signals. Neither row mentions uncertainty or bits.
Communication here links sender, signal, shared code and receiver. AI4K12 rows on the structure and ambiguity of language cover the code in the human case and where computers struggle with it.

Intuitive Theories are folk physics, folk biology and folk psychology formed without instruction. AI4K12 row 4-B-i lists naive physics and folk psychology as knowledge a computer would need. Folk biology and development are absent.

Theory of Mind is representing another's goals and beliefs. AI4K12 row 4-B-i lists folk psychology as knowledge a computer would need. Row 4-C-i covers recognizing feelings, which the concept does not include, so it is left out. False-belief tasks have no row.

Agency here is sensing a setting and responding flexibly toward aims. AI4K12 row 4-D-i asks whether machines understand or are conscious. Row 1-B-i, on perception, covers only the sensing half, so it is left out. Organism agency has no row.
The AI sense of Knowledge is a store of statements a program searches. AI4K12 rows on domain knowledge and on schemas in knowledge graphs cover it. Knowledge held by people and groups has no row.

Technology here covers tools made and adopted in every domain. AI4K12 rows on AI in daily life and on AI's effects on sectors of society treat one family of tools and what follows from using it. They do not define technology.

The AI sense of Culture is machine culture, a proposed extension. AI4K12 row 5-B-i covers AI in daily life and the debates it raises. The shared ground is that AI products shape what people see and make. The row uses 'culture' for a society's norms.

Norms are shared expectations upheld by a group's approval. AI4K12 row 5-A-iii asks designers to learn the norms and values of the groups an AI system serves. Norms as a topic in themselves have no row.
Institutions are stable rules with arrangements that apply them. AI4K12 row 5-B-ii asks students to judge which uses of AI deserve regulation, and regulation is an institution. The row stays on AI.

Descent is drawn as a branching tree, and borrowing between lines turns it into a network. AI4K12 rows on trees and graphs teach those two diagram forms as data structures. The match covers the diagram form only. Ancestry has no row.

ai4k12Unaligned.why: Comparing human and animal perception. I2:3-5 compares how species act and learn, and its Agency definition includes sensing. Adding a senses comparison there would cover this item.
Computer sensing compared with human sensing. Pair it with the item above in I2:3-5 so that animal, human and device senses sit in one comparison.

Humans combining information from several senses. The cognition sense of Information (sensory input and a receiver whose expectations change) could carry a 6-8 stage on how nervous systems and sensors combine signals.
Perception as extracting meaning from sensory signals. Information separates a cue, a signal and meaning across biology, cognition and AI. A 3-5 stage on Information could cover this.
A vision system lacking knowledge of objects from other cultures. I1:6-8 covers culture as transmitted knowledge. A case on what a system trained in one culture misses would cover it.

interdisciplinaryAdds.adds: Animals copy and are helped by others (biology), children learn from adults and peers (cognition, education), and machines fit patterns in data. The comparison brings in teaching and scaffolding, which machines lack.

Organisms regulate behavior toward goal-states with no awareness (biology). Software has goals set by designers (computation). People have intentions (cognition). Together students sort goal-directed, aware and designed apart.

A graded agency scale from bacterium to human to recommendation system replaces a yes or no question about machine minds. It draws on biology, cognition and computation and asks what each rung can and cannot do.

Children already explain actions by wants (developmental cognition). Comparative biology asks whether apes do the same. Robots lack this knowledge (computation). The cross-domain view treats it as a skill that develops, with a different history in machines.

Students test a rule as human hypothesis testers (cognition, education) and reflect on confirming versus refuting. A supervised learner has no such reflection. The comparison shows what a person does that a fitting procedure does not.

People search by small changes to a known solution (cognition), cultures keep stocks of solved examples (culture), and programs search defined states (computation). The reading shows search with and without a stated list of options.

Anthropology and sociology explain why values differ: norms are passed on by social learning and upheld by approval (culture, cognition). That gives the AI design question a source for the differences it asks designers to respect.

Collective intelligence and distributed cognition (culture, technology) give mechanisms for how a platform changes what a group knows. AI4K12 names the cultural challenge. The stage explains how copying, selection and tools produce it.

A cue carries information that nobody sent (biology), a text carries meaning that can mislead (culture), and a message carries bits (computation). The cross-domain view separates signal from meaning before asking what perception extracts.

A reward signal in machine learning matches payoffs that shape animal choices (biology) and prices or grades that people weigh (culture). People understand incentives. Animals and programs only respond. A badly set reward is followed faithfully.

Species trees, language trees and manuscript trees (biology, culture) show when a tree fits and when borrowing makes a network. Students choose between a tree and a graph for a given set of relations.

A map is a stand-in (culture, education), a mental image is a stand-in (cognition), and a stored vector is a stand-in only for a user who reads it that way (computation). The cross-domain view asks who treats the thing as a stand-in.
